Chapter 3: Language, Stories, and the Subtle Shaping of Identity
Let’s dive into something we might not notice every day—the way words and stories shape how kids see themselves and the world around them.
Language isn’t just a bunch of words we use to talk. It’s more like a mirror, reflecting the values and ideas of the culture we live in. Think about the way we speak to children, the books they love, even the shows they watch. All of these things quietly teach them what’s possible, what’s accepted, and what’s worth striving for.
One of the best ways to support feminist values is by being really intentional with our language. What does that look like? Well, it means moving away from phrases that lock kids into old stereotypes. Instead of always telling girls they’re “pretty” or describing boys as “strong” in a way that suggests they have to be tough, why not focus on qualities like creativity, kindness, or determination? These are strengths anyone can have, and kids need to hear about them.
Now, let’s talk about stories—the ones we tell at bedtime, read in books, or watch on screen. Classic tales often show us princesses waiting to be rescued and heroes bravely conquering all kinds of challenges. Sure, they’re fun, but they also send quiet signals about who gets to act, who makes choices, and whose stories matter. By mixing in books and movies that feature all kinds of characters and adventures, we can help kids imagine a world where anyone can be the hero.
This doesn’t mean tossing out every traditional story. Instead, it’s about adding some context and sparking conversation. When you read a fairy tale where a prince saves a princess, try asking, “What else could the princess have done?” or “Maybe the prince needed help too—what do you think?” These simple questions invite kids to think beyond the usual script and see that stories aren’t set in stone.
The influence doesn’t stop with words and stories. Media and toys also shape how kids see themselves. Look at toy aisles or TV ads—girls’ toys often focus on beauty and caring, while boys’ toys are all about action and building. But what if we just let kids pick what interests them, instead of steering them toward something just because of their gender? That’s a powerful way to break down artificial barriers.
Here’s something else to pay attention to—the small stuff, those little everyday interactions that add up. Compliments, jokes, even quick remarks can shape what a child believes about themselves. If a girl keeps hearing she’s “so helpful” and a boy always gets praised for being “so smart,” it can quietly steer how they see their own strengths. Being aware of these patterns helps us create a more balanced, encouraging environment.
So, what does this look like in real life? It might mean:
- Picking out books and shows with strong, diverse girls and boys who show their feelings. - Using words that celebrate all kinds of qualities, in all kids. - Encouraging children to ask questions and talk about the stories they hear. - Letting kids choose toys and activities based on what excites them, instead of what’s labeled for boys or girls.
By paying attention to the language we use and the stories we share, we’re helping kids build a sense of identity that’s flexible and confident—not boxed in by old ideas about gender. And that’s a gift that lasts a lifetime.
